Where it began

He was born in Bridgetown, Barbados, on 28 July 1936, the fifth child in a family of six. As a boy he would play any game with a ball in it: cricket, football, basketball. By 13 he was turning out for a club side, and in the nets he bowled left-arm spin at grown men, a West Indies Test player among them.

He first played for Barbados at 16, in 1953, and took seven wickets on debut. A year later, still only 17, he was in the Test side against England at Sabina Park. They picked him as a bowler. He took a wicket in his first over.

The player

His figures still look like a misprint. In 93 Tests he made 8,032 runs at 57.78, with 26 hundreds, and took 235 wickets. He also held 100 catches, mostly close to the bat. From 1965 he led West Indies in 39 Tests, and his first series in charge brought their first series win over Australia.

The innings everyone remembers came in Kingston in 1958. Against Pakistan he went to his first Test hundred and simply kept going, to 365 not out, a new world record. He was 21. In England in 1966 he was so dominant with bat and ball that people started calling him King Cricket.

What made him special

He did everything left-handed and nearly everything well. With the new ball he bowled quick and late swing; later in the day he could switch to orthodox spin, or to wrist spin with a googly tucked away. At the crease he picked the length early and moved his feet like a dancer. In Swansea in 1968, captaining Nottinghamshire, he became the first man to hit six sixes in an over in first-class cricket. An 11-year-old boy found the last ball in a garden and later handed it back to him.

If there was a gap in the record, it was that the wickets came steadily rather than in heaps. He never took ten in a Test match. When you are asked to be three bowlers at once, that seems a fair price. It took him a while, too, to turn early starts into big scores. Then he turned his first one into 365.

Away from the middle

He played league cricket for Radcliffe in Lancashire, helped South Australia win the Sheffield Shield and captained Nottinghamshire. He was a good enough footballer to play at left-back in Barbados, and his favourite sport of all was golf. He was knighted in 1975, became one of the National Heroes of Barbados in 1998, and the ICC named its Player of the Year award after him. He died in July 2026, aged 89.

And finally

On his first tour of England, in 1957, he found the spring so cold that he often wore two or three jumpers at once. And in 1967 he wrote a cricket novel for young readers in which a university side becomes unbeatable with the help of computer analysis. Most captains of his day would have settled for picking him.
